concepts.title: Gangadharpant's Jolt into Another History
concepts.definition: Professor Gaitonde, a historian of five books, meets a bus collision in Pune and wakes in an India that never was: the East India Company defeated at Panipat, Maratha power intact, and Bombay a Maratha-ruled city. His scientific 'adventure' is Jayant Narlikar's device for asking what history is and how it might have differed.
concepts.key_idea: One collision, two histories -- the professor crosses from what happened into what might have been.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb105.txt opening sections (gaitonde historian, bus collision, alternative history india, panipat outcome reversed)

solution_steps.explain: A collision with a bus flings the professor between worlds, landing him in a parallel India.
Panipat was lost by the Company, the Marathas rule, and English influence is checked -- history took another road.
As a historian he resists wonder and hunts evidence -- library, books, records -- to test the impossible.

concepts.title: Evidence Hunting: Library, Books and the Maratha World
concepts.definition: In the Asiatic Society library Gaitonde finds his own five-volume history rewritten in six volumes, with the third recording a Maratha victory at Panipat and treaties that ended Company ambitions. Town names, currency and Rajavidyalaya's absence confirm a self-consistent world -- fiction built on real historical possibility.
concepts.key_idea: A consistent other-world proves the point: history had live alternatives, and Panipat was one hinge.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb105.txt library sections (asiatic society library, sixth volume, panipat victory of marathas, treaties, rajavidyalaya, evidence of parallel world)

solution_steps.explain: His familiar five-volume history exists with a different third volume -- the first hard evidence.
Marathas win Panipat; the Company is confined, treaties redirect trade, and India modernises without subjugation.
Streets, institutions and accounts all corroborate, showing Narlikar's alternate history as coherent counterfactual, not fantasy.

concepts.title: The Science Behind the Adventure: Quantum Reality
concepts.definition: The story's turn to science comes through Rajendra Deshpande, who invokes quantum theory: reality at its base is probabilistic, so the same past can branch into different worlds. Cataclysmic events -- like the collision -- may flip awareness from one branch to another; the lacking world can even pop in and out of existence.
concepts.key_idea: Physics lends the mystery a ladder -- probability, branching worlds and missing matter explain the impossible journey.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb105.txt science sections (rajendra deshpande, quantum theory, catastrophe theory, lack of matter, world popping in and out, british readers tom barker mention)
question_patterns: how does quantum theory explain gaitonde's experience

solution_steps.explain: Rajendra reminds Gaitonde that quantum physics replaced certainty with probability -- many outcomes possible from one past.
The bus accident serves as the cataclysm that shifted the professor's consciousness into the branch where Panipat was won.
The unaccounted matter missing from experimental records even allows worlds to pop in and out -- fiction resting on real physics talk.

worked_examples.question_pattern: What single document most convinces Gaitonde that he is in a parallel world, and why does it convince him?

solution_template.explain: The third volume of his own history, containing a Maratha victory at Panipat he never wrote.
As author he knows his text; a materially different edition of his own book cannot be misremembered.
The book anchors the parallel world in his own scholarship, making the counterfactual vivid and believable.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Rajendra says reality is probabilistic. Explain how this idea supports the story's central adventure.

solution_template.explain: At the quantum level, events resolve from a spread of possibilities; certainty belongs only to measurement.

solution_template.action: scale it up in the story
solution_template.explain: Narlikar extends this to worlds: both Panipat-outcomes existed as possibilities, each realised in its own branch.
His collision let his mind cross branches -- the adventure becomes a thought experiment on probability and history.
